description: PostgreSQL Performance Monitoring Dashboard using CloudEye (SberCloud) metrics. This dashboard provides comprehensive monitoring for PostgreSQL RDS instances with full observability coverage matching CloudEye. KEY SECTIONS: - Connection Analysis: Active connections, idle transactions, and connection metrics - Query Performance: Transaction throughput, slow SQL queries, and query performance - Database Performance & Resources: CPU usage, memory usage, IOPS, network throughput (input/output), system memory hit rate, CPU breakdown (user/kernel/wait), swap metrics, disk I/O operations, latency, and throughput - Locks & Blocking: Lock waiting sessions monitoring - Transactions: Long-running transactions (alive/idle/2PC), oldest transaction duration, and maximum database age - Replication & WAL: Replication lag, WAL size, replication slot usage, replication status, inactive slots, and synchronous replication blocking time - Disk Space & Usage: Total disk size, used space, free space, usage percentage, and inode usage - Database Activity & I/O: Row operations, disk read/write throughput, I/O latency, IOPS breakdown, disk I/O wait time, and audit log size DATA SOURCE: Metrics are collected via prometheus-cloudeye-exporter from SberCloud CloudEye service.

panels.description:
Replica status over time. Shows when the replica was Up (1) or Down (0).

**What it shows:**
- 1 = At least one replica is Up and replicating
- 0 = No active replicas (replication is down)

**How to read:**
- Green area = Replica is Up
- Red area = Replica is Down
- Timeline shows exact times when status changed
- Helps identify replication failures and downtime periods

**Note:** The raw metric value is 2 (master + 1 replica), but we check if it's > 0 to show replica status.
panels.title: Replica Status

panels.description:
Master database instance status over time. Shows when the database was Up (1) or Down (0).

**What it shows:**
- 1 = Database is Up and responding (CPU or Memory utilization > 0)
- 0 = Database is Down (no CPU/Memory activity detected)

**How to read:**
- Green area = Database is Up
- Red area = Database is Down
- Timeline shows exact times when status changed
- Helps identify downtime periods and incidents
panels.title: Master DB Status

panels.description:
Connection pool utilization ratio (0.0-1.0). Shows how close PostgreSQL is to running out of connections.

GOAL: Stay below 70% utilization during normal operation
- < 0.7 (70%): Healthy
- 0.7-0.8: Monitor closely, plan capacity increase
- > 0.8: Critical - take immediate action

ACTIONS TO IMPROVE:
1. Implement connection pooling (PgBouncer, Pgpool-II)
2. Reduce application connection pool sizes
3. Increase max_connections (requires RAM)
4. Fix connection leaks (check idle_age metrics)
5. Enable idle_in_transaction_session_timeout

KUBERNETES TIP: max_connections >= (num_pods x connections_per_pod) + 20% buffer
panels.title: Connection Pool Utilization

panels.description:
PostgreSQL performance degrades with **100+ ACTIVE connections**, regardless of max_connections setting.

**Common K8s Problem:**
- Pods autoscale -> connection pools multiply
- Result: Massive IDLE connections flooding the database
- Even with low active, total connections exhaust resources

**What to watch:**
- ACTIVE = Actual queries running (alert when >100)
- IDLE = Wasted connections from pod scaling
- IDLE IN TRANSACTION = Critical (holding locks)

**Solution:** Use PgBouncer for connection pooling in K8s

**Alert on:** Active > 100, NOT percentage utilization!

panels.description:
Total number of current user connections to the database. Shows all user connections including active and idle states.

**What it shows:**
- Total current user connections (includes both active and idle)
- Different from "Active Connections" which shows only actively executing connections
- Helps monitor overall connection pool usage from user applications

**Note:** This metric shows all current connections (385 in your case), while "Active Connections" shows only those executing queries (14 in your case).
panels.title: Active Connections of Users

panels.description:
Maximum transaction duration across all connections. Shows the oldest active transaction.

**Alive vs Idle:**
- **Alive** = Transactions actively executing queries (doing work)
- **Idle** = Transactions waiting/idle (not executing, may hold locks)

**Two-Phase Commit (2PC):** Used for distributed transactions across multiple databases. Monitors long-running 2PC transactions that may block other operations.

**GOAL:** No transactions running >5 minutes
- Long transactions block vacuum, cause bloat
- Long queries may indicate missing indexes or inefficient SQL
panels.title: Long-Running Queries

panels.description: Idle connections by age - detect connection leaks
panels.title: Idle in Transaction Connections (Total - No Age Breakdown)

panels.description:
Transactions **actively executing queries** for more than specified duration. High values indicate blocking transactions.

**Alive** = Transaction is actively running SQL queries (doing work)
**Idle** = Transaction is waiting/idle (not executing, may hold locks)

High values indicate transactions that are taking too long to execute.
panels.title: Transactions Alive (Long-Running)

panels.description:
Sessions waiting for locks. Shows how many database sessions are blocked waiting for locks to be released.

**What it shows:**
- Number of sessions waiting for locks (row-level, table-level, etc.)
- High values indicate lock contention
- **0 = No blocking (healthy state - this is normal!)**
- If you see 0 consistently, it means your database has no lock contention issues

**Why monitor?**
- Lock contention can severely impact performance
- Indicates potential deadlocks or long-running transactions holding locks
- Helps identify blocking queries

**Note:** It's completely normal to see 0 for extended periods if your application doesn't have lock contention.
panels.title: Wait Events

panels.description:
Transactions **waiting/idle** (not executing queries) for more than specified duration. High values may indicate connection leaks or transactions holding locks.

**Alive** = Transaction is actively running SQL queries (doing work)
**Idle** = Transaction is waiting/idle (not executing, may hold locks)

High values indicate idle transactions that may be holding resources.
panels.title: Transactions Idle (Long-Running)

panels.description:
Two-Phase Commit (2PC) transactions running for more than specified duration.

**What is 2PC?**
Two-Phase Commit is used for distributed transactions across multiple databases/resources. It ensures atomicity across different systems.

**Why monitor?**
- Long-running 2PC transactions can block other operations
- Indicates potential issues with distributed transaction coordination
- High values may indicate network issues or resource contention

**Alive vs Idle:**
- **Alive** = Transaction actively executing queries
- **Idle** = Transaction waiting/idle (may hold locks)

**Note:** **It's completely normal to see 0 if your application doesn't use distributed transactions (2PC).** Most PostgreSQL applications don't use 2PC unless they're coordinating transactions across multiple databases or systems.
panels.title: Two-Phase Commit Transactions

panels.description:
Maximum duration of the oldest active Two-Phase Commit (2PC) transaction. Shows the longest-running 2PC transaction.

**What is 2PC?**
Two-Phase Commit is used for distributed transactions across multiple databases/resources. It ensures atomicity across different systems.

**What it shows:**
- Duration of the oldest active 2PC transaction
- High values indicate long-running distributed transactions
- May indicate network issues or resource contention in distributed systems

**GOAL:** No 2PC transactions running >5 minutes
- Long 2PC transactions can block other operations
- Indicates potential issues with distributed transaction coordination

**Note:** **It's completely normal to see 0 if your application doesn't use distributed transactions (2PC).** Most PostgreSQL applications don't use 2PC unless they're coordinating transactions across multiple databases or systems.
panels.title: Oldest Two-Phase Commit Transaction Duration

panels.description:
Database activity overview showing two key metrics on separate axes:

**Active Connections (left y-axis, green line):**
- Number of currently active database connections
- Connections that are actively executing queries or transactions
- Shows database load from concurrent users/applications
- Measured in: Count of connections

**Transactions/sec (right y-axis, yellow line):**
- **What it means:** Number of database transactions executed per second (TPS - Transactions Per Second)
- **Why right axis:** Uses a different scale (0-600+ transactions/sec) than connections (14-16), so it's displayed on a separate right-side Y-axis for better readability
- Measures database workload intensity and query throughput
- Higher values indicate more database activity and processing load
- Helps identify peak usage periods, batch jobs, and performance bottlenecks

**How to read the graph:**
- **Left Y-axis (green):** Read Active Connections count (typically 14-16)
- **Right Y-axis (yellow):** Read Transactions/sec rate (typically 100-700)
- Both metrics are plotted on the same timeline, allowing you to correlate connection count with transaction rate
- Example: If you see a spike in Transactions/sec but stable Active Connections, it means the same connections are processing more transactions (higher throughput)
panels.title: Active Connections & Query Rate

panels.description:
Total count of slow SQL queries over the selected time range. Shows queries exceeding 1 second and 5 seconds thresholds.

**Note:** CloudEye does not provide per-query details, only aggregate counts.

**Difference from 'Long-Running Queries':**
- **Slow SQL Queries** = Count of queries that exceeded time thresholds (counters)
- **Long-Running Queries** = Duration of the oldest active transaction (gauge)

If Slow SQL shows 0 but Long-Running shows data, it means:
- There are long-running transactions, but CloudEye may not be counting them as 'slow queries'
- Or the slow_sql metrics may not be collected/enabled in CloudEye
panels.title: Slow SQL Queries

panels.description:
Transaction throughput - number of transactions executed per second. Shows database workload intensity.

**What it shows:**
- Higher values = More database activity
- Spikes indicate periods of high load
- Helps identify peak usage patterns

panels.description:
Percentage of memory cache hits. Shows how often data is found in memory cache vs disk. Higher values (closer to 100%) indicate better performance.

**What it shows:**
- 100% = All data served from memory (ideal)
- <95% = Some data read from disk (may indicate insufficient memory)
- Values > 100% are capped at 100% (may occur due to measurement artifacts)

panels.description:
Maximum transaction age in the database. Shows the age of the oldest transaction ID. High values indicate need for VACUUM.

**What it shows:**
- Number of transactions since the oldest active transaction
- Values in millions (e.g., 41.8 Mil = 41,800,000 transactions)
- Increasing trend indicates database is aging

**Why monitor?**
- High age (>1 billion) can cause transaction ID wraparound issues
- Indicates need for VACUUM or VACUUM FREEZE
- Critical for database health and preventing wraparound failures

**Thresholds:**
- < 1 billion: Healthy
- 1-2 billion: Warning (plan VACUUM)
- > 2 billion: Critical (immediate VACUUM required)

Number of active stream replication replicas. Shows the count of active read replicas connected to the master database.

**What it shows:**
- Number of active replicas (typically 1 in your setup)
- Value 1 = One replica is active and replicating
- Value 0 = No active replicas (replication is down)

**Note:** The raw metric value is 2, but we subtract 1 to show the actual replica count (excluding the master instance).

panels.description:
Number of sessions waiting for locks by database and lock mode. Shows lock contention across databases.

**What it shows:**
- Number of sessions waiting for locks (row-level, table-level, etc.)
- Breakdown by database and lock mode
- High values indicate lock contention
- **0 = No blocking (healthy state - this is normal!)**

**Why monitor?**
- Lock contention can severely impact performance
- Indicates potential deadlocks or long-running transactions holding locks
- Helps identify blocking queries and databases with high contention

panels.description:
Total size of each database in bytes.

GOAL: Monitor growth trends, plan capacity
- Sudden growth: investigate unexpected data
- Steady growth: normal, plan storage scaling

ACTIONS TO IMPROVE:
1. Identify large tables (pg_total_relation_size)
2. Archive old data
3. Partition large tables
4. Drop unused indexes
5. Run VACUUM FULL on bloated tables (maintenance window)
6. Consider table compression (TOAST settings)
